BUSINESS STRATEGIES AND FUTURE PLANS
Our Group aims to strengthen our position as a logistics operator in the ASEAN region and the
PRC. To achieve this, our Group intends to focus on the following strategies and future plans.
Establish a digitalised and technology-driven Mega Depot in Singapore to provide integrated
logistics services
In recent years, the Singapore government has been promoting innovation and sustainable industrial
development in favour of smart facilities and better land use. According to the Frost & Sullivan, the MPA
has highlighted digitisation and sustainability as their priorities. To further such objectives, the MPA has
begun the construction of the next-generation Tuas Megaport which is expected to increase operating
efficiency and reduce emissions.
To align with the Singapore government’s plan of consolidating port operations to the Tuas
Megaport and to support our strategy to be an integrated logistic solution provider, we are strategically
transitioning from operating depots across different locations in Singapore towards an integrated and
high-capacity Mega Depot that will occupy approximately 80,000 sq.m. of land (strategically located in
close proximity with the Tuas Megaport), which upon completion, will be the largest consolidated
container depot facility in Singapore and second largest in Southeast Asia according to Frost & Sullivan.
Since 2017, we have been in discussion with Party C, a statutory body in Singapore which is
involved in the development and management of industrial estates and their related facilities in
Singapore, for the development of the Mega Depot. The Group had engaged professional consultants
including an architect, quantity surveyor, traffic consultant and project management company, to assist
with the development of the Mega Depot, including providing technical knowledge and carrying out
preliminary studies for discussion with Party C to, amongst others, determine the size of land required.
After years of discussion and based on our proposed designs, (SG) EK Logistics, a subsidiary of our
Group, had entered into an agreement for lease with Party C in 2020 in respect of necessary land for
development of the Mega Depot. Under the agreement for lease, we have been offered to lease relevant
land from Party C upon satisfaction of certain investment and building requirements at which point a
written lease agreement will be formally executed. A summary of the salient terms of the agreement for
lease (and the lease of the land) is set out below:
Location: 30 Tuas South Avenue 10, Singapore
Usage: Container depot, warehouse and ancillary office
Approximate area: 80,000 sq.m
Term of lease: 30 years from the commence date of 16 December 2020
Specific obligations: Investments of a minimum amount on new plant and machinery
as well as completion of construction of all buildings,
structures and installations on the land by December 2026
187

=== PAGE 197 ===
BUSINESS
The development plans for the Mega Depot has been formally approved by Party C in November
2023 following (i) a comprehensive review of the project requirements to ensure that the Mega Depot
would be designed and built to meet industry standards of safety, efficiency, and sustainability; and (ii)
the obtaining of research support and input from the National University of Singapore on its design,
which is expected to use both automatic container stacking cranes and mobile container stackers to
balance our needs for additional handling capacity and operational efficiency in the Mega Depot.
As a major transshipment hub, our Directors are of the view that Singapore would not be materially
impacted by the U.S. tariff developments and believes that the Mega Depot will solidify our position as a
leading container depot operator in Singapore in terms of container throughput in 2025 in light of the fact
that, according to the Frost & Sullivan Report, one of the key barriers in Singapore’s container depot
industry is land constraints; which has led to increasing challenges for container depot operators to obtain
long-term lease of land with close proximity to major port terminals for their operations. Our Directors
believe that our latest development and technological designs are consistent with the Singapore
government’s direction and goal to achieving land productivity in Singapore.
Based on the approved Plans, the Mega Depot will include a warehouse with a net lettable area of
approximately 36,500 sq.m and a container depot of a capacity of approximately 23,000 TEUs under one
roof in the same location with extensive implementation of IT systems. The Mega Depot will represent a
high-density solution (with a handling capacity that exceeds the operational limits of 95% of individual
private depots in Southeast Asia) that is aligned with the sustainability goals of the Singapore
government. By interfacing automated hardware with predictive software and the implementation of
digitalised technological developments, the Mega Depot will function as an integrated ‘‘smart’’
ecosystem that reduces turnaround times for processing containers and will serve to position us
competitively amongst other logistic service providers in the region. This "smart" design of the Mega
Depot also responds to the lease condition agreed with Party C for the Group to implement an automated
lifting technology at the Mega Depot with the aim of intensifying container depot land use through the
deployment of digitalised, automated and technology-driven solutions for its container depot operations.
Given the size and location of the Mega Depot, we plan to expand our range of services in Singapore by
offering laden container storage services (including laden reefer container storage) to consignees in the
future (which will serve to save time for shippers in hauling empty containers from the container depot to
the warehouse (for loading) and then hauling the laden containers from the warehouse to the container
port terminal).
Our Mega Depot will be situated approximately seven kilometres from the gate of Tuas Megaport
and approximately eight kilometres from the Singapore-Malaysia border. With two storeys, the Mega
Depot will have four-high automated container stacking on the ground floor and nine-high stacking on
the upper floor, allowing us to meet the objective of achieving 13-high stacking in total in accordance
with our Plans. Our design is to have stacking cranes on the ground floor to achieve greater operational
turnaround and to deploy container stackers on the upper floor for slower moving containers. Doing so
allows us to balance our need for additional handling capacity while achieving operational efficiency.
The reason for utilising a combination of automated and non-automated system is to allow operational
flexibility and to maximise utilisation of space when demand surges.

We have engaged an independent design and build main contractor in connection with the
construction of the Mega Depot, which was selected following completion of relevant tender process in
February 2025. The construction of the Mega Depot has commenced in mid-February 2025 and is
expected to be completed by the end of 2026 based on the existing plans with the design and build main

Based on the approved Plans, the Mega Depot will consist of two storeys comprising (i) non-
automated empty container storage area; (ii) elevated warehouse area (i.e. warehouse area on the ground
floor); (iii) automated storage area for laden and empty container storage; and (iv) office space for our
operations. With a view to increasing storage capacity, the Mega Depot will implement innovative
technological developments and progressive automation into key aspects of our container depot
operations including, amongst others, gate entry and survey as well as container placing and yard
management.
Our Mega Depot in Singapore with the planned integration of a ‘‘smart’’ ecosystem is expected to:
(i) consolidate the services we provide in Singapore under one roof; (ii) increase our container depot
handling capacity; (iii) reduce turnaround times for processing containers for our container depot
operations through the use of automation and other technologies, thereby increasing our efficiency and
reducing the possibility for human error; (iv) position ourselves competitively amongst other logistic
service providers in Singapore as an integrated logistic solution for container and logistic service needs
through the expansion of our range of offerings to additionally provide warehousing and laden container

Utilisation of new technology to reduce our greenhouse gas emissions and resource consumption
To better manage our environmental, social and climate-related risks, we aim to reduce our
greenhouse gas emissions and resources consumption in the foreseeable future by upgrading existing
machineries into electric vehicles. In particular, we anticipate purchasing a range of 10 to 15 electric
container stackers over the next three years to replace some of our existing diesel powered container
stackers because (i) electric container stackers have lower resource consumption and require lower
maintenance as compared with diesel powered container stackers; and (ii) the use of electric container
stackers will reduce our Group’s carbon emissions which is in line with the Group’s overall strategy on
ESG matters as well as the global shift towards sustainability and green technology.
We are also able to reduce our resource consumption and carbon footprint through the utilisation of
our IT systems such as our cashless payment technologies and handheld survey systems. These IT
systems allow us to reduce certain processes in our workflow and create more streamlined services to our
customers.

Red Sea crisis
The Israel-Gaza war, a regional crisis in the Red Sea, emerged since late 2023 leading to
disruptions in maritime trade and causing geopolitical uncertainties. The Red Sea crisis persists as of the
Latest Practicable Date.
Impact on industry
According to the Frost & Sullivan Report, the escalation of tensions in the Red Sea region has
impacted canal capacities in key shipping routes such as the Suez Canal resulting in extended delivery
times with vessels having to re-route via the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa. The Red Sea crisis
forced vessels on the Europe-Asia route to take a longer route around the Cape of Good Hope causing
disruptions to shipping networks and congestion at shipping ports globally. The lengthened delivery
times has contributed to delays in container availability and scheduling inefficiencies, leading to a
reduction in effective global container shipping capacity.
With the Suez Canal being a critical conduit for approximately 30% of the world’s container traffic,
the Red Sea crisis has since been causing surges in freight rates. By way of example, according to the
CCFI, there was a volatile but general upwards trend in early 2024, where freight rates in February 2024
had increased approximately 36% as compared to February 2023. The impact of the Red Sea crisis
showed signs of easing in 2024, leading to a slight decrease in the CCFI during the year.
Impact on our business operations
A summary of the key impact of the Red Sea crisis on our business operations during the Track
Record Period is set out below:
(i) Container depot operations. The reduced global container shipping capacity caused by the
Red Sea crisis led to increased container demand generally, which resulted in less container
storage demand at our container depots in 2024. As a result, our storage fees revenue
decreased from approximately S$15.8 million for the year ended 31 December 2023 to
approximately S$8.0 million for the year ended 31 December 2024.
194

=== PAGE 204 ===
BUSINESS
Based on our Directors’ understanding, the Red Sea crisis also led to container shipping lines
leasing more containers from container leasing companies in 2024 to meet their container
demands, in which relevant container leasing companies had approved more units for repair in
preparation for use to cater for the increased on-hire demand. This resulted in an increase in
our repair and maintenance in terms of TEU from 550,000 TEU for the year ended 31
December 2023 to 560,000 TEU for the year ended 31 December 2024.
(ii) Warehousing and CFS. The Red Sea crisis did not materially impact our warehousing and CFS
business during the Track Record Period.
(iii) Container sales and new-build container inspection. Our revenue generated from the
provision of container sales and new-build container inspection services increased from
approximately S$1.5 million for the year ended 31 December 2023 to approximately S$9.1
million for the year ended 31 December 2024, which was mainly attributable to the increase in
demand in containers as well as new-build container inspection services from certain
customers during 2024 as a result of the Red Sea crisis prolonging vessel sailing times from
the West back to Asia. This led to a lack in supply of empty containers to meet exporting
demands from Asian countries resulting in the need to purchase and/or manufacture containers
to meet their needs.
(iv) Freight forwarding services in Qingdao. The spike in freight rates in early 2024 as a result of
the Red Sea crisis had corresponding impacts to our freight forwarding services in Qingdao.
Specifically, our revenue generated from the provision of freight forwarding services
increased from approximately S$20.3 million for the year ended 31 December 2023 to
approximately S$34.3 million for the year ended 31 December 2024.
Our Directors are of the view that the effects of the Red Sea crisis, such as prolonged vessel sailing
times from the West back to Asia which had impacted our Group’s business operations during the Track
Record Period, will likely remain for a while after any ceasefire and/or conflict resolution given that
container shipping lines typically prefer a more cautious approach and have established alternative routes
to mitigate risks.
U.S. tariff developments
During the second half of 2024, the incoming U.S. Trump administration signalled the possibility of
significant tariff increases on imports of Chinese goods which resulted in increased global trading
activities ahead of the impending tariffs. Since inauguration of President Donald J. Trump in early 2025,
the U.S. Trump administration has advocated greater restrictions on international trade.
On 2 April 2025, the current U.S. administration introduced a new set of reciprocal tariffs, starting
with a baseline of 10% and increasing for nations with significant trade deficits with the U.S.. Major
trading partners like the PRC, Vietnam, South Korea and the European Union have been significantly
impacted. Since then, the U.S. administration has announced a series of bilateral framework agreements
with certain partners, with terms varying from affirmed tariff rates to preferential rates or country-
specific exemptions. As between the U.S. and China, a series of trade truces has been announced in 2025,
including a 90-day reduction in bilateral tariffs to 10% on each other’s goods (from 125% in April 2024)
which has been extended until November 2026.
195

=== PAGE 205 ===
BUSINESS
The legality of the U.S. tariffs, invoked by the president of the U.S. under the International
Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), was challenged in a series of proceedings in the U.S. court
systems, and was ultimately ruled unconstitutional by the U.S. Supreme Court and the collection of
increased duties has stopped since 24 February 2026. The president of the U.S. responded by invoking
section 122 of the U.S. Trade Act of 1974, setting a 10% global tariff to take effect on 24 February 2026
(expiring after 150 days), which was later threatened to be raised to 15% although such change has not
been officially documented. On 7 May 2026, the U.S. Court of International Trade ruled that the broad
application of the section 122 surcharges to be unlawful, although such ruling is subject to appeal and the
tariffs are duly to expire in July 2026. On March 11, 2026, the U.S. administration launched
investigations against 16 trading partners (including Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam)
regarding alleged excess industrial capacity and forced-labour concerns under section 301 of the U.S.
Trade Act of 1974, the results of which may give rise further tariffs which is not subject to statutory rate
cap or expiry unlike section 122. On April 8, 2026, the U.S. President further threatened, via social
media, an additional 50% tariff on imports from any country found to be supplying military weapons to
Iran, and on April 12, 2026 publicly indicated that this threat would extend to China; as of the date of this
prospectus, no implementing executive order, proclamation or U.S. Customs and Border Protection
guidance has been issued, and the legal authority for any such tariff remains uncertain following the
Supreme Court ruling.
The timeline and scope of the U.S. tariffs remained fluid, with implementation subject to continued
negotiations between the U.S. and its trading partners. The unpredictability of tariff adjustments and
possible retaliatory actions by nations persists as at the Latest Practicable Date.
Impact on Industry
According to Frost & Sullivan, the uncertainty of tariff changes between the U.S. and the PRC are
examples of geopolitical events which influences the ongoing volatility in global shipping and supply
chains.
Following the announced 90 days reprieve on the U.S. tariff war in around May 2025, container
bookings from the PRC to the United States have surged considerably as U.S. importers and other market
participants stock up inventory, raw materials and Chinese goods as part of their frontloading efforts in
order for manufacturers, distributors and retailers to catch up with backlogged orders as well as plan for
anticipated future demand. This has led to an increase in freight rate caused by congestion, delays and
challenges in securing cargo space.
Following the initial shock phase in early 2025, global trade proved more resilient than anticipated
with many affected Chinese exporters successfully diverting shipments to other markets. Despite a
decline in direct exports to the U.S., China’s total export value increased by 5.6% year-on-year in 2025
and trade surplus reached a record US$1.2 trillion, as it continues to advance its export-driven model and
deepen trade relations with its trading partners, with expansion of shipments to other regions such as
Europe, Latin America and other Asian economies. In the first quarter of 2026, China reported a 6.2%
year-on-year increase in total social logistics value (reaching 96.4 trillion yuan) despite the persistence of
protectionist tariffs, due to the rapid expansion of high-value manufacturing and a strategic shift in trade
toward ASEAN and Belt and Road partners. Many Asian countries are increasingly acting as re-export
hubs and extended manufacturing bases. Countries such as Vietnam, South Korea and others are
expanding their manufacturing capacity as companies implement ‘China plus one (or two)’ strategies,
196

=== PAGE 206 ===
BUSINESS
and takes on larger role in assembly and re-export of Chinese parts. Whilst U.S. and Europe takes efforts
to reduce dependency on China, diversify supplier sources and stock up on inventories to mitigate risks,
China’s production base is often simply too large to substitute for local resources and supplies. In
practice, most relocations are occurring within Asia rather than re-shored to Europe or other higher-cost
regions. Due to the above, liners and freight forwarders are rebalancing networks and shifting capacity to
less tariff-sensitive corridors (such as, Latin-America-Europe, or intra-Asia).
It would appear therefore that, in the near term, the diversion of U.S.-bound sourcing away from
China toward Southeast Asia, together with the lower current section 122 U.S. tariff rate relative to the
previously announced country-specific IEEPA rates, has supported export volumes and led to sustained
growth in container throughput in the jurisdictions in which we operate. In particular, the Port of
Singapore recorded an 8.5% year-on-year increase in container throughput and Malaysia recorded a
10.4% and 12.7% year-on-year increase in external trade and exports volume respectively during the first
quarter of 2026, despite the imposition of protectionist tariffs, primarily due to regional supply chain
rerouting and the sustained global demand for essential high-tech components beyond the US market.
Should country-specific tariffs be reintroduced under section 301 following the expiry of the
section 122 measure however, or should the threatened secondary tariff connected to the Iran conflict be
implemented against China or other countries in the region, shipping volumes on the Transpacific and
intra-Asia trade lanes could potentially decline. That said, trans-shipment-focused operations in
Singapore and Malaysia are, by their nature, less directly exposed to any single bilateral tariff, as a
significant majority of cargo throughput handled are transhipment as opposed to export-related (although
they remain vulnerable to carrier decisions about where to call and how much capacity to deploy which
could be affected by changes to Transpacific demand due to tariff disruptions).

Outlook
While available operational and financial data of the Group appears to suggest that the tariff
disputes between the U.S. and major economies across the global has had a limited impact on our
operations and results of operations, our Directors believe that the U.S. administration may continue use
tariffs as a central lever of its trade strategy which, coupled with global geopolitical events (such as
ongoing wars and U.S. ambitions to exert control over various geographical territories), will continue to
strain global trade and give rise to supply chain uncertainties. This may continue to impact trade flows
and transhipment volumes in the jurisdictions in which the Group operates and may have implications on
our financial and operational performance as our business is intricately linked to global trade flows.
Our Directors expect, and the Joint Sponsors (having reviewed all relevant information - including
analysis of available operational data of the Group and the views on expressed by Frost & Sullivan on
U.S. tariff policies on the shipping and container depot industries) concur, that the business operations
and financial results of the Group should remain relatively unscathed from evolving U.S. tariff polices,
taking into account the complementary nature of its various business income streams. That said, we will
continue to monitor and assess how developments concerning U.S. tariff policies impact our business,
and we will prudently adapt our operations (such as to adjust our container depot capacity in jurisdictions
where we operate) accordingly.

(PRC) QD Port Lianyun will reimburse (PRC) QD Keyun
for the remaining rental payments for the relevant premises.

=== PAGE 210 ===
BUSINESS
Commercial rationale for the joint venture arrangement
Our Directors believe that the joint venture arrangement is an efficient means to further our Group’s
business in the PRC given that partnering with the Qingdao Port JV Partner would (i) help strengthen the
Group’s relationship with Qingdao’s government-owned port operator, being a key player in the local
market; (ii) enhance the Group’s reputation within the industry and the region; and (iii) allow the Group
to leverage such strategic partnership, as the Directors are of the view that the Qingdao Port JV Partner
can lead the Qingdao container depot business from a level of strength as the controlling shareholder
given their track record and history of providing a wide-range of port-related services ranging from basic
port services, such as stevedoring and storage services, to ancillary and extended services such as
logistics services and financing-related services, and therefore enabling our Group to provide more
comprehensive services to container shipping line companies.
Financial and operating impact
Pursuant to the joint venture arrangement, we agreed to transfer all our existing container depot and
warehousing and CFS business in Qingdao (which was conducted through (PRC) QD Keyun) to (PRC)
QD Port Lianyun with such transfer completed in or around March 2024 (the ‘‘Business Transfer’’). Our
Directors’ are of the view that the joint venture arrangement is proceeding well and in line with their
expectations.
The Directors and the Joint Sponsors are of the view that the Business Transfer should not have
any material adverse impact on the Group’s financial performance and position going forward based on
the following analysis:
(i) prior to the Business Transfer, the revenue derived from the transferred business only
accounted for approximately 2.9% and 2.6% of the Group’s total revenue for the years ended
31 December 2022 and 2023, respectively;
(ii) the revenue of (PRC) QD Keyun was not adversely impacted by the Business Transfer, and in
fact had actually increased from approximately S$23.7 million for the year ended 31
December 2023 (which included container depot and warehousing and CFS business) to
S$32.9 million for the year ended 31 December 2024 (which did not include container depot
and warehousing and CFS business) despite transferring out the container depot and
warehousing and CFS business;
201

=== PAGE 211 ===
BUSINESS
(iii) (PRC) QD Keyun did not materially contribute to the overall financials of the Group over the
Track Record Period, having recorded a modest loss of approximately S$1.0 million for the
year ended 31 December 2023 (the loss was mainly attributable to impairment loss in the
amount of S$1.2 million resulting from the suspected fraud incident concerning the
subsidiary’s freight forwarding business in Qingdao). Following the Business Transfer, (PRC)
QD Keyun (excluding the container depot and warehousing and CFS business which was
transferred to (PRC) QD Port Lianyun for most of the year) recorded a nominal loss of
approximately S$0.3 million (including impairment loss in the amount of S$0.4 million
resulting from the same suspected fraud incident) for the year ended 31 December 2024
whereas, it recorded return from interest in association in the amount of approximately S$0.2
million for the year ended 31 December 2024;
(iv) as the machinery and equipment of (PRC) QD Keyun had already been substantially
depreciated (with the net asset value of such machinery and equipment amounting to only
approximately S$0.1 million) as at 31 December 2023, the transfer of the business with an
effective disposal of relevant machinery and equipment did not have significant impact on the
net asset value of the Group;
(v) as a result of the Business Transfer, right of use assets of approximately S$167,000 and lease
liabilities of S$201,000 were derecognised from our financial accounts resulting in the
recognition of a net gain of S$34,000; and
(vi) the employment contracts of relevant staff of the transferred business were transferred to
(PRC) QD Port Lianyun as part of the Business Transfer and, as such, the Group will not
continue to bear associated staff costs.
Prior to carrying out the Business Transfer, we informed customers who used our container depot,
warehousing and CFS and freight forwarding services in Qingdao of the Business Transfer and, based on
our understanding and knowledge, none of our customers have ceased to engage our Group or (PRC) QD
Port Lianyun as a result of the Business Transfer.
MARKETING
We consider that our success depends to a significant extent on the goodwill of our brands and
reputation in the shipping industry as one of the leading container depot operators in Southeast Asia and
a trustworthy service provider. Successful branding through marketing strategies is vital for us to
establish our brand recognition and awareness for attracting new customers and retaining existing ones.
Our sales, marketing and commercial team is headed by our group marketing general manager, Mr.
CHAN Terry Tat-lee. Our marketing, commercial and business development strategy is primarily
centered on maintaining our established key customer relationships as well as fostering long-term
relationships with prospective customers. As such, our sales, marketing and commercial team actively
reaches out to potential new customers for new prospects while maintaining relationships with existing
customers through regular service calls and customer meetings and engagements.

BUSINESS
Our executive directors, sales, marketing and commercial team and operations staff have maintained
relationships with our existing customers who are mainly container shipping lines and container leasing
companies. Our staff are encouraged to put forward a range of solutions to our container depot customers
by offering a full range of container and logistic solutions to cater to their logistics needs which include,
amongst others, suggestions to utilise our value-added services such as container depot services, logistic
related support services and container sales and new-build container inspection services where most
suitable. In particular, our container sales business utilises our network of agents and suppliers to assist
our customers, which are container shipping lines and container leasing companies, in the sale of their
used containers.
Our sales, marketing and commercial team will coordinate with our existing and potential
customers for our operations staff to provide training, demonstrations and information sessions. Most of
our customers are long-term returning or referred customers, which helps us maintain close relationships
and develop new business opportunities through the loyalty built by our Group’s relationship. We believe
our high-quality container depot and logistics services and good relationships are key to both retaining
our existing loyal customers and attracting new ones.
Our customers are typically focused on the reliability and efficiency of our services, and in this
regard, we believe that our experience, reputation and track record have enabled us to market ourselves
successfully and effectively to our customers throughout the years.
CUSTOMERS
Our customers mainly comprise container shipping lines, container leasing companies and freight

Pricing Policy
In determining our Group’s pricing policy, we consider a variety of factors which are set out below
by types of services.
207

=== PAGE 217 ===
BUSINESS
Container depot operations
Storage and The Group will charge its customers based on market rates which are
handling services generally determined by factors including, without limitation, (i) type of
container; (ii) depot capacity; (iii) market demand; (iv) location; (v) number
of containers stored monthly; (vi) labour cost; and (vii) prevailing market
rates.
Repair and The Group will charge its customers for any container parts required for
maintenance services repair and maintenance based on costs of the container part plus a reasonable
profit margin. For repair and maintenance work, the Group will charge its
customers based on market rates which are generally determined by factors
including, without limitation, (i) nature of work; (ii) cost of materials; (iii)
labour cost; (iv) type of container; (v) location; and (vi) prevailing market
rates.
Transportation services The Group will charge its customers based on market rates which are
generally determined by factors including, without limitation, (i) fuel cost;
(ii) labour cost; (iii) distance required for transportation; and (iv) prevailing
market rates.
Warehousing and CFS
Warehousing The Group will charge its customers based on market rates which are
and CFS generally determined by the factors including, without limitation, (i) nature
of the goods; (ii) duration of cargo storage; (iii) weight; (iv) volume; (v)
location; and (vi) prevailing market rates.
Container sales and new-build container inspection
Container sales The Group will charge its customers based on costs of the containers sourced
plus a reasonable profit margin which are generally determined by factors
including, without limitation, (i) supply and demand of containers; (ii)
condition of the container at the point of sale; (iii) delivery charges (if any);
and (iv) prevailing market rates.
Container survey The Group will charge its customers based on market rates which are
services generally determined by factors including, without limitation, (i) complexity
of survey criteria; (ii) type of container; (iii) manpower required; (iv) labour
cost; (v) location; and (vi) prevailing market rates.
208

=== PAGE 218 ===
BUSINESS
Other
Freight forwarding The Group will charge its customers based on costs plus a reasonable profit
services margin which takes into account, without limitation, (i) ocean freight charges
which include costs of container space on vessels and varies depending on the
shipment origin and destination, nature of cargo, weight of the cargo and
volume of the cargo; (ii) local charges, such as handling, transportation,
documentation and customs clearance charges; (iii) overseas logistics
charges; and (iv) prevailing market rates.
Final prices will generally be formulated on a case-by-case basis in line with market prices and
after a price negotiation process.
Credit Policy
We generally grant a credit period ranging from 30 to 60 days from the invoice date, but variations
may occur on a case-by-case basis subject to the approval by our management, taking into account: (i)
customer’s background, reputation and credibility; (ii) customer’s payment history in the industry; and
(iii) customer’s business relationship with us.
Our Group reviews our customer payment records from time to time and, if necessary, will revise
the credit terms accordingly. Our customers have been continuously settling their bills without default
and our Directors consider that there was no collectability issue in relation to such outstanding trade
receivables. During the Track Record Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date, we did not experience
material default in payment from our customers. Our trade receivable turnover days during the Track
Record Period are within the credit period.
Customer Service
We understand that providing outstanding customer service is important to upholding our Group’s
market reputation and nurture customer loyalty. Our sales, marketing and commercial team contacts
potential customers through phone or email to sell our products or services. A large number of our new
customers are referred from existing customers or other logistic service providers that we work with. Our
operations staff handle customer inquiries, service bookings, and feedback. We handle general enquiries
and feedback on a location-by-location basis and also follow up closely with customers on their orders
and level of satisfaction.
In case of complaints, our operations staff are required to report such complaints to the head of
sales and marketing team immediately where they will follow up with the complaint directly. We also
review the business workflow to improve our services from time to time.
Our Directors have confirmed that our Group had not experienced any material complaints from our
customers and did not have any disputes with them during the Track Record Period.

BUSINESS
SEASONALITY
Our business operations are generally not subject to seasonality changes. However, as a container
depot operator with operations across the ASEAN region and the PRC, our business is intricately linked
to global trade flows and the movement of containers across the world. Our business is directly tied to the
volume of containers passing through our facilities. As such, we closely monitor and analyse the trends
and patterns in the global shipping market to ensure we are well-positioned to capitalise on container
movements such as the increasing trade flows between the PRC and South East Asia given the trend of
manufacturers relocating their operations to South East Asia to take advantage of lower costs and in
response to increasing geopolitical tensions.
SUPPLIERS
During the Track Record Period, suppliers to our Group mainly included container shipping lines,
reefer equipment manufacturers, freight forwarders and lessors. We have a diverse supplier base and we
believe there is no individual supplier concentration risk. For the years ended 31 December 2023, 2024
and 2025, our five largest suppliers in each year accounted for 24.3%, 29.5% and 30.3% of our total cost
of revenue, respectively, of which the largest supplier accounted for 6.0%, 9.9% and 18.4%, respectively.
Our five largest suppliers in each year during the Track Record Period are Independent Third Parties. Our
Group has maintained business relationships of approximately 10 to 37 years with our five largest
suppliers in each year during the Track Record Period. Our suppliers, excluding our lessors, generally
grant us credit terms ranging from 21 to 60 days. The availability of credit and the credit terms extended
to us by our suppliers vary from supplier to supplier. Under most of our leases, we are required to pay our
lessor in advance of each month without a credit period.

Subcontracting arrangements
During the Track Record Period, we have engaged subcontractors for the provision of certain
services as our Group in certain jurisdictions does not possess sufficient (i) prime movers for
transportation of empty containers; (ii) labour for repair and maintenance of containers; and (iii)
warehousing services. We may occasionally engage certain service providers on a one-off basis to
facilitate urgent needs of which such payment terms generally range from cash upon delivery to seven
days credit period. For the years ended 31 December 2023, 2024 and 2025, our subcontracting expenses
for trucking and transportation amounted to approximately S$5.4 million, S$4.5 million and S$4.5

S$6.9 million, S$5.9 million and S$5.3 million, respectively, which represented approximately 6.3%,
4.9% and 5.0%, respectively.
When selecting our subcontractors, based on the nature of the subcontracting, we evaluate carefully
based on their (i) qualification and certification; (ii) capacity and availability; (iii) quality and timely
performance of subcontracted works; (iv) pricing; and (v) reputation. We had not experienced any
difficulty in identifying and engaging subcontractors when required. For our subcontracting
arrangements, we typically inspect the completed work by our subcontractors on a job-by-job basis and
record any issues detected. Our Directors are of the view that such subcontracting arrangements are
common within the container depot industry and allows us to utilise our own labour more efficiently,
reduce our operational costs and better manage our resource allocation.

Overlapping of customers and suppliers
We provide services and products to parties in the logistic supply chain including container
shipping lines and container leasing companies as well as freight forwarders. As such, some of our
customers are also our suppliers, or vice-versa.
 For container shipping lines and container leasing companies, we may provide container depot
services to them in respect of our container depot business (as our customers) and they may
sell us used containers in respect of our sale of containers business (as our suppliers). We may
also engage container shipping lines to provide container space aboard their vessels in respect
of our freight forwarding business (as our suppliers).
 For reefer equipment manufactures, we may provide reefer repair and maintenance services to
them as their authorised service centre (as our customers) and they may sell us reefer parts (as
our suppliers).
 For freight forwarders, we act as local freight forward agent for overseas freight forwarders
(as our customers) who (i) rely on our local expertise, know-how (including in terms of
familiarity with regulations, customs processes and infrastructure) and relationships
(including with warehousing and CFS facilities) which enables smoother operations and
enhance efficiency in the supply chain; and (ii) rely on us to consolidate shipments from
multiple forwarders to achieve economies of scale and to promote efficiency. Similarly, we
procure the services of overseas freight forwarding agents (as our suppliers in respect of our
freight forwarding business) to leverage on their offshore knowledge, know-how and expertise
to promote efficiency in servicing our customers. Given the nature of the freight forwarding
business, it is not uncommon for customers and suppliers to overlap.
In respect of our freight forwarding business, we have established a network of logistic service
providers to handle and execute customer orders. This network includes, amongst others, other freight
forwarders and local transportation companies to provide related logistics services where the other party
has presence or capability. For our business operations in the PRC, Tianjin Zhongke Group had been both
a customer (in respect of our freight forwarding business in Qingdao and warehousing and CFS business
in Qingdao and Tianjin) and a supplier (as a subcontractor providing trucking services and office rental
for our container depot business in Tianjin) of our Group during the Track Record Period. The members
of Tianjin Zhongke Group are Independent Third Parties (and previously our connected persons up to

TRANSFER PRICING ARRANGEMENT
Transfer pricing assessment
The Singapore Income Tax Act establishes the legal requirement for related party transactions to be
carried out at arm’s length, and the Comptroller of Income Tax of Singapore may enforce the arm’s
length principle and make necessary adjustments to the taxable profits of a Singapore taxpayer if the
transactions with its related parties are not carried out on an arm’s length basis. Under the ninth edition of
the Singapore Transfer Pricing Guidelines (the ‘‘Singapore TP Guidelines’’) published by the Inland
Revenue Authority of Singapore (‘‘IRAS’’), Singapore taxpayers are required to maintain adequate
documentation on contemporaneous basis to demonstrate that reasonable efforts have been made to
determine that pricing of cross-border related party dealings are consistent with arm’s length principle
(i.e. that transactions between related parties should be conducted on similar terms to those that would
have been agreed had those parties been dealing independently from one another in otherwise similar
circumstances. Although Singapore is not a member of the OECD, the IRAS endorses the arm’s length
principle and accepts the definition thereof endorsed by the OECD which are set out in its transfer
pricing guidelines (the ‘‘OECD TP Guidelines’’)
In order to ensure compliance with the relevant transfer pricing regulations, we have engaged an
independent tax service firm as part of an international professional accounting firm in Singapore, to
provide transfer pricing documentation services to ascertain and document the arm’s length nature of
material related party arrangements of the Group.
The relevant material related party arrangements of the Group involve (SG) EK Marketing, as a
marketer and promotor of the Group’s container deposit services to our global or regional customers
(being responsible for the development and maintenance of customer relationships as well as securing
business contracts and annual tariff renewal with these customers) procuring the following affiliated
entities of the Group (all of which are fellow subsidiaries of (SG) EK Marketing) to provide the various
container depot services (as set out below) to our customers, whereunder part of the revenue received
from our customers is reimbursed as service fee payments to these related affiliated entities for services
rendered (the ‘‘Covered Transactions’’):

Based on the functional analysis performed, it was substantiated that (SG) EK Marketing may be
characterised as a provider of marketing and promotion services which benefit (and are of economic or
commercial value to) the related party container depot service providers, and in its performance of such
function, (SG) EK Marketing bears various risks (including market price and volume, marketing, foreign
exchange, inventory and customer credit risks) associated with the normal course of its business. It was
also observed that the services provided by (SG) EK Marketing are typically chargeable, centralised
activities under the OECD TP Guidelines.
Of the transfer pricing methodologies to test the arm’s length nature of related party transactions,
the transactional net margin method (‘‘TNMM’’) was determined to be the most appropriate method for
testing the Covered Transactions. The TNMM compares the net profit margins realised by (SG) EK
Marketing in its role as a marketing entity with the net profit margins of comparable entities dealing
independently. The economic analysis performed by using the TNMM involved the identification of
comparable companies in the ASEAN region, Australia, the PRC, Hong Kong, India, Japan, South Korea,
New Zealand and Taiwan which engaged in similar marketing service functions as those performed by
(SG) EK Marketing and reviewing their weighted average inter-quartile range of net cost plus margins
(‘‘NCPM’’). Based on such analysis in the transfer pricing documentation reports for the financial years
ended 31 December 2023 to 31 December 2025, (SG) EK Marketing’s NCPM of 9.37%, 9.43% and
9.11% for the financial year ended 31 December 2023, 2024 and 2025 are within the inter-quartile range
of NCPM achieved by the set of independent comparable companies.

MARKET AND COMPETITION
The container depot business is highly competitive and we are confronted by aggressive
competition in all areas of our business. Generally, the barriers to entry of the container depot industry
are high as the industry is capital-intensive, and often constrained by the lack of land space in certain
countries in which we operate.
Although we have observed a few container shipping lines entering into the container depot
business through investing in their own container depots, they may still use the services of other
container depots to alleviate space constraints at their own container depots. As such, we believe we are
able to capitalise on our independence to ensure competitiveness amongst other container depots that may
be partnered with or wholly-owned by container shipping lines. Please refer to the paragraph headed
‘‘Risk Factors – We operate in a highly competitive industry and may be exposed to increased
competition and potential loss of market share as container shipping lines continue to expand into the
container depot business in the locations in which we operate’’ in this prospectus for further details.
In order to mitigate the abovementioned risk, we seek to provide independent container depots
services through diversifying our customer base and working with multiple container shipping lines,
container leasing companies and relevant logistic service providers. We also strive to maintain tenured
relationships with our existing customers, including those container shipping lines that operate their own
container depots, by providing high quality services including accommodating customers’ ad-hoc
requests for additional storage space for empty containers, and facilitating customers’ requests for
handling specific kinds of containers such as reefer containers.
Through our competitive strengths as set out in the paragraph headed ‘‘Competitive Strengths’’ in
this section above, our Directors believe that we compete favourably with our competitors in the markets
that we operate in.

INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY
IT is integral to our operations and to the quality and competitiveness of our container and logistic
related businesses. Our Group utilises IT systems for various operation and functional needs, including
sharing of operational data and reports with our customers and providing our customers with payment
options. Our key IT systems are as follows:
 Container Management System. Our container management system is designed and developed
to support our container depot operations. Our system enables us to track and update container
movements through a centralised system and also allows our customers to obtain the location
details and inventory information of their containers in real time through a web-based
platform and through an instant electronic data interchange which is linked to our customers’
internal systems. It also allows for the provisions of up-to-date information on repair
estimates, revenue collection status and generation of customer and operation reports. We
utilise this container management system in all our container depots across the ASEAN region
and the PRC which provides transparency and instantaneous updates to our customers,
ensuring that crucial data such as delivery details are always up-to-date. We actively work
with our customers to set up such electronic data interchanges which can be tailored to
provide specific information and parameters as required by our customers. We believe the
ability to integrate our system with our customers’ internal systems via instant electronic data
interchange with the use of industry standards (such as CEDEX, CODECO, WESTIM and
COPARN) is a factor which our customers appreciate.
 Depot Appointment System. Our container depot appointment system allows hauliers to make
advanced appointments for the pick up or return of containers at our container depots.
Together with our container management system, we are able to have up-to-date and accurate
information on our container depot utilisation to ensure that appointments are well managed
and our resources are deployed accordingly to manage our container depot demands. This
system also enables us to manage traffic congestion at our container depots which improves
the overall efficiency and productivity of our container depot operations.
 Handheld Survey. Our handheld survey systems support our container survey and inspection
services which are part of our container depot operations business as well as our container
sales and new-build container inspection business. Such handheld survey systems include our
handheld survey app and our customised handheld survey system for reefer containers. Our
handheld survey app is part of our IT initiative to digitise the container survey process. Our
handheld survey app digitises the previously paper-based survey process, generating cost
estimates in real time upon completion of surveys. The handheld device also allows for all
weather operations as it is IP68 rated. Our customised handheld survey system for our reefer
serving business allows us to carry out inspection and survey of reefer containers through
interfacing with the onboard electronics for diagnostics by our specialised staff. This allows
our staff to identify repair and maintenance works that may be necessary internally which
would otherwise not be apparent upon physical inspection only. The addition of handheld
survey in the container survey and inspection process enables us to have a higher accuracy
rate as well as improve the turnover time required to conduct the survey and inspection of a
container.
227

=== PAGE 237 ===
BUSINESS
 B.I. On The Go. This system allows our staff to access key business data as well as trending
and analysis information anywhere via mobile application. Our staff who are frequently on the
move or work remotely can access this system to stay connected to the Group’s data and
insights at all times. The ability to access this information anytime and anywhere means that
our staff can respond quickly to changing circumstances and make informed decisions on the
go.
 Gate Automation System. The gate automation system uses the information gathered from the
license plate recognition system and the depot appointment system to automatically validate,
process and facilitate faster gate entry of prime movers when they arrive at and exit the depot.
The license plate recognition system utilises advanced cameras and optical character
recognition (OCR) technology to identify prime movers with valid license plates as they enter
the depot. The gate automation system is also equipped with the automatic seal dispenser,
which is the first to be implemented in Singapore (according to the Frost & Sullivan Report),
where drivers can collect the container seal from the dispenser upon exiting. The gate
automation system is able to leverage the database in our existing container management
system and enable us to minimise data entry, capture feedback from operations accurately and
streamline relevant administrative and validation processes at the gate. The system also
eliminates the need for drivers to leave their vehicles and shortens the turnaround time for
prime movers to drop off or pick up containers from the previous 30-minute manual standard
to a general average of approximately nine minutes. This system has been implemented in our
depots located in Singapore and it is expected to be implemented in all of our depots
regionally starting with Hong Kong and Thailand in the year 2026.
During the Track Record Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date, we did not experience any
failure in our IT systems which caused material disruptions to our business operations. We are, however,
susceptible to risks relating to failure of our electronic system and database. Please refer to the paragraph
headed ‘‘Risk Factors – We are dependent on our electronic management systems and we may suffer from
information and technological system failures which could have material and adverse impacts on our
business’’ in this prospectus for further details.
We have established an internal manual to govern our IT systems, which includes protocols and
procedures for internet access, backups, electronic communications, activity logging and virus control as
well as contingency measures. Our IT department manages disaster recovery activities and repeatable
functions such as backups and system monitoring, while firewalls are implemented to safeguard our
internal networks. By maintaining these controls, we are confident that we can mitigate the risk of system
failure and provide a secure and efficient electronic data exchange environment for our business
operations. Moving forward, we will continue to enhance our IT systems to support our long-term
growth and serve a wider customer base.

INSURANCE
As a provider of logistics services, our business inherently carries a number of risks, including
vehicle collisions, cargo loss or damage, property loss, and business interruptions due to natural disasters,
political unrest, or other factors. To manage these risks, we maintain a range of insurance policies at both
global and local operational levels. These policies provide coverage for third-party liability,
transportation risks, property loss and damage, workers’ compensation for injury and death, and other
areas. By maintaining this comprehensive insurance coverage, we are able to mitigate potential financial
losses and protect our business from unforeseen circumstances.
As at the Latest Practicable Date, we maintain comprehensive insurance policies to cover, among
others, our risks relating to: (i) industrial all-risks; (ii) property all-risks; (iii) fidelity guarantee and
money insurance; (iv) work injury compensation; (v) motor vehicle; (vi) crime; (vii) corporate liability;
(viii) hospitalisation and accidents; (ix) comprehensive general liability; and (x) cyber related risk.
Our Directors are of the view that our insurance coverage is sufficient and aligns with industry
standards. As we continue to expand our business, we will regularly review and reassess our risk
portfolio. This will enable us to adjust our insurance practices in accordance with our evolving needs and
prevailing industry standards. By doing so, we will ensure that our insurance coverage remains
appropriate and effective in mitigating potential risks to our business. For details, please refer to the

coverage may not be sufficient in covering the risks or losses that may result from our operations’’ in this
prospectus for further details.

ENVIRONMENTAL, SOCIAL AND GOVERNANCE
ESG Governance
We acknowledge our environmental protection and social responsibilities and are aware of the
climate-related issues that may impact our business operations. We are committed to promoting
sustainable development and ESG reporting requirements upon Listing.
Our Board has overall responsibility for overseeing and determining our Group’s environmental,
social, and climate-related risks and opportunities impacting our Group, establishing and adopting the
ESG policy and targets of our Group, and reviewing our Group’s performance annually against the ESG
targets and revising the ESG strategies as appropriate if significant variance from the target is identified.
We have established an ESG policy with reference to the requirements set forth in Appendix C2 to
the Listing Rules and an ESG committee that comprises our management representatives who are
responsible in respect of ESG related matters in different operation locations in which we operate. The
ESG committee serves as a supportive role to our Board in implementing the agreed ESG policy, targets
and strategies; identifying and assessing ESG-related matters, including climate-related risks, by taking
into consideration the metrics and targets stipulated in Appendix C2 to the Listing Rules and applicable
laws, regulations and industry standards; managing how our Group adapts its business in light of climate
change; collecting ESG data from different parties while preparing for the ESG report; and continuous
monitoring of the implementation of measures to address our Group’s ESG-related risks. The ESG
committee reports to the Board regularly on the ESG performance of our Group and the effectiveness of
the ESG systems upon Listing.
Climate Change Impact and Mitigation Measures
Communities around the world are gradually becoming more and more concerned with climate
change and greenhouse gas emissions. Climate change has resulted in harsh weather, which we believe
poses a certain level of threat to us. There are two major types of climate risk, which are physical risk
and transition risk.
i. Physical risk: It is the direct risk arising from weather related events and changes in weather
patterns. We believe that climate-related issues may bring about the risk of increasingly
severe extreme weather events, such as more frequent heatwaves, storms, typhoons and
flooding. We may potentially be affected by disruption of container depot operation, injuries
to employees during work, risks related to non-performance and delayed performance.
ii. Transition risk: It is the risk arising from the transition to a carbon neutral economy. We
believe that our customers may shift their preferences to a sustainable lifestyle because of
climate change and global trends to reduce carbon emissions to facilitate transition to a low-
carbon community. Therefore, we may face transitional risks that would require us to move
towards a sustainable business model. For instance, we may need to upgrade existing
machinery into electronic vehicles, which could result in increased operational costs. In
addition, regarding increasing responsibilities on emission disclosure, we may be affected by
increased cost to execute more stringent monitoring measures on emission and resources
consumption.
231

=== PAGE 241 ===
BUSINESS
To mitigate climate-related risks such as more frequent extreme weather conditions, we have
followed the guidelines issued by Ministry of Manpower of Singapore in all our operation locations, for
example, we would wait at least 30 minutes after thunder is heard before resuming work. In addition, we
would suspend immediately all outdoor work in exposed areas where employees are liable to be
endangered by adverse weather conditions such as rainstorms and thunderstorm. In addition, in order to
prevent water logging caused by heavy rains in the rainy season, which may harm the equipment and
employees’ safety, we would inspect the drainage system in advance to ensure that channels are
unblocked.

cleaning cost to seek for customer’s approval via email. Based on the type of stains, different types of
chemical washing detergent are used to wash the containers. For example, some stains require two or
three time cleaning process for eliminating the stains totally.

Work Safety
Cargo handling activities are one of the highest sources of potential accidents in our container depot
operations. Inexperienced workers can cause punctures or dents and containers or stack them unevenly, or
drop them. Hence, to maintain a safe and healthy environment at work, the following key measures have
been in place:
 a workplace Safety and Health (‘‘WSH’’) policy has been established to promote positive
workplace safety culture;
 a workplace Safety and Health Committee has been established to monitor, support and review
the implementation of the health and safety issues;
 safety signs are shown as an alert or reminder to staff about particular hazards, e.g. forklifts
operating in a particular area: they also remind staff about correct procedures to be followed,
such as speed limits or requirements to wear correct personal protective equipment when
undertaking tasks;
 proper personal protective equipment (such as safety helmets, reflective vests, glove safety
rubber boots and safety goggles) are provided where appropriate;
 occupational safety meetings are held on monthly basis so that the safety manager would
discuss any potentially unsafe acts, share the best practice and enhance staff’s awareness of
safety issues with the depot-in-charge and the contractor representative;
235

=== PAGE 245 ===

 onsite inspection are conducted by safety manager to identify unsafe acts, equipment, tools,
structure and other conditions at workplace, to ensure any identified issues are rectified;
 for those operators of mechanical equipment and vehicles, human resources personnel is
responsible to check if valid certificates have been received before employment to ensure the
workers have the necessary knowledge, skills and techniques for carrying out the work using
mechanical equipment;
 the travelling speed of mechanical equipment and vehicles are specified and restricted to
ensure traffic safety. Safe speed limit signs are prominently displayed so as to ensure the
operators are aware of them; and
 to ensure safety in using mechanical equipment, such as forklift truck, front loader, reach
stacker, gantry crane, tower crane, mobile crane, the equipment would be inspected by

Workplace safety and health inspections and continuous improvement
Our container depots in Singapore are subject to periodic inspections by the MOM in the ordinary
course of our operations to ensure a safe working environment. In December 2024, the MOM carried out
a workplace safety and health inspection at our container depot located at 61 Tuas South Street 5,
Singapore (the ‘‘Inspection’’), following which the MOM identified two areas for improvement at the
depot, namely (i) that the safe working loads of the container stands used at the repair areas operated by
two of our resident sub-contractors be determined by a competent person and prominently displayed on
the relevant container stands for workers’ information; and (ii) that containers stored near the boundary
of the depot be positioned at least six metres from the fence-line, or otherwise in a configuration that
complies with the recommended parameters under Singapore Standard SS 684:2022 (Code of Practice for
Container Depot Operations) (‘‘SS 684:2022’’) (together, the ‘‘Suggested Areas of Improvement’’). The
Inspection did not arise from, and was not associated with, any accident, injury or damage.
238

=== PAGE 248 ===
BUSINESS
We responded promptly to the issues and arranged for the Suggested Areas of Improvement to be
implemented. Subsequently, the MOM informed us that the matter was closed off and that no further
action would be taken.
Following the foregoing, we reviewed and readjusted the storage configurations across all of our
container depots in Singapore for compliance with SS 684:2022, and implemented additional internal
control procedures requiring proper handling of excessive inflow or intake of containers, which has been
reviewed by our independent internal control consultants.
Service Quality
Quality is important in attracting and retaining customers. To provide quality services to customers,
we have a centralised container management system to let the customers reserve a timeslot for pick-up or
drop-off. It could facilitate our planning work and avoid a long queue of trucks outside the container
terminal. We also offer customers electronic data interchange functionality through both EDI and API, so
the customers can have access to accurate and up-to-date container statistical reports to help the
customers make more timely and informed decisions about their operations. We have established a
complaint handling policy so that our operations staff are required to report complaints to the department
head. Department head shall then fill in the Incident Report and determine what kind of remedial actions
shall be taken and communicate with the customers directly. In addition, department head shall determine
what kinds of preventive actions shall be taken for continuous improvement promptly. The remedial
actions and preventive actions shall be documented in the Incident Report and signed by the Department
Head and pass to ESG committee for record keeping.
Supply Chain Management
During the Track Record Period, suppliers of services to our Group mainly included container
shipping lines, reefer equipment manufactures, freight forwarders and lessors. In view of the growing
social concern about environmental issues, we are aware of the importance of managing the
environmental and social risks of its supply chain. We selected suppliers based on different aspects, such
as their machine capacity and quality, cost, reputation, past dealings experience and the environmental
and social risks. We will continue to monitor our supply chain in terms of environmental and social
standards. During the Track Record Period, we are not aware of any environmental or social non-
compliance committed by our major suppliers.
Data Protection
The Group manages and protects the data collected from its business partners, customers,
employees, and suppliers to safeguard their confidentiality. Information systems security policy and data
protection policy have been formulated to ensure a robust framework around data protection across the
Group. According to the policies, all desktop computers and notebooks shall be protected by a firewall
and anti-virus software. Also, all desktop computers and notebooks must utilize passwords to prevent
unauthorised access. The policies also specified that any action that may expose the company to risks of
unauthorised access to data, disclosure of information, legal liability, or potential system failure is
prohibited and may result in disciplinary action up to and including termination of employment and/or
criminal prosecution.

We are committed to fostering a fair, ethical and efficient working environment by abiding by the

NON-COMPLIANCE
Save as disclosed below, our Directors are of the view that we had complied with all relevant laws and
regulationsinallmaterialrespectduringtheTrackRecord Period and up to theLatestPracticableDate:
FailuretocompleterelevantconstructionformalitiesfortheSubjectBuildings
Backgroundandreasonsfornon-compliance
Asmentionedintheaboveparagraph“Legalproceedinginitiatedagainst(PRC)TJKeyun”,wehadpreviously
failed to complete the relevant construction formalities prior to, during and upon completion of the construction of
theSubject Buildings. Thefailureto completetherelevant construction formalities was due to the failureof thethen
landlord, Tianjin Port Logistics to obtain the real estate certificate of the Subject Land. However, as Tianjin Port
Logistics,asthelandlordandlessor,wasnotusuallytheresponsibleorleadingpartyinconductingsuchconstruction
formalities, it might not be possible to directly seek any recourse against Tianjin Port Logistics in this regard. On 9
October 2019, Tianjin Municipal Urban Management Committee (天津市城市管理委員會) imposed an
administrative fine of RMB1,164,395 on (PRC) TJ Keyun for our failure to obtain the construction planning permit
(建設工程規劃許可證) prior to the construction of the Subject Buildings, which we duly paid on 16 October 2019.
On7March2024,TianjinBinhaiNewAreaHousingandConstructionCommittee(天津市濱海新區住房和建設委員
會) imposed an administrative fine of RMB179,400 on (PRC) TJ Keyun for our failure to conduct the construction
acceptance check (竣工驗收) for the Subject Buildings before putting the Subject Buildings into use. (PRC) TJ
Keyundulypaidthefineon 8March 2024.
The Subject Buildings were constructed on the Subject Land leased from Tianjin Port Logistics.
However, Tianjin Port Logistics did not actually obtain the relevant land use right of the Subject Land at
the time of construction of the Subject Buildings. As such, it was not possible for (PRC) TJ Keyun under
relevant PRC laws and regulations to apply for, go through and complete relevant construction
formalities, and ultimately, apply for and obtain the real estate certificate of the Subject Buildings.
Rectification actions and potential impact on us
On 27 March 2024, (PRC) TJ Keyun obtained the real estate certificate of the Subject Land and the
Subject Buildings until after (PRC) TJ Keyun had duly paid the penalty for the failure to conduct the
construction acceptance check for the Subject Buildings before putting the Subject Buildings into use, as
under normal conditions, the completion of construction acceptance check would be the necessary
prerequisite in applying for the real estate certificate under applicable PRC laws and regulations.

Failure to register lease agreements with relevant PRC government authorities
Background and reasons for non-compliance
As at the Latest Practicable Date, we had nine leased premises located in various cities in the PRC,
of which four lease agreements (‘‘Lease Agreements‘‘) had not been registered with the relevant PRC
government authorities. Pursuant to the Measures for Administration of Lease of Commodity Properties
《( 商品房屋租賃管理辦法》), the lessor and the lessee of a lease agreement are required to file the lease
agreement with relevant government authorities within 30 days after the execution of the lease agreement
and obtain property leasing filing certificate for the lease agreement. Although we had reached out to our
lessors of the Lease Agreements for their necessary support with regard to the filing of the Lease
Agreements, they have not provided us with the relevant documents in order to complete the filings.
Rectification actions and potential impact on us
As advised by our PRC Legal Advisers, the failure to register the Lease Agreements with the
relevant PRC government authorities does not affect the validity of the Lease Agreements, but the
relevant PRC government authorities may require us to complete registration within a specified
timeframe, and if we fail to so rectify, we may be subject to a fine ranging from RMB1,000 to
RMB10,000 for each of the Lease Agreements, and we may be subject to a maximum penalty of
RMB80,000 for the failure to register the Lease Agreements.

Failure to obtain land use certificate for the property in which we carry out container depot
operations in Vietnam
Background and reasons for non-compliance
As at the Latest Practicable Date, we operate a container depot in Dong Nai province, Vietnam
under a service agreement with a local container depot operator from 1 May 2023 to 30 April 2026 and
has been automatically renewed for one year pursuant to the service agreement. The local depot operator
provides the land for us to carry on our container depot operations in the Dong Nai province, but has not
obtained the appropriate land use right certificate for us to carry out such container depot operations as at
the Latest Practicable Date.
The state authorities in Vietnam decide on land use purposes through land use (master) plan, and
permits for land use conversion. A parcel of land is broadly classified as either (i) agricultural (e.g. land
for aquaculture or cultivation of perennial crops or annual crops); or (ii) non-agricultural (e.g. urban or
rural residential land, commercial and service land). The specific type of land is specified in the land use
right certificate issued by the state authorities, and it is strictly prohibited to use the land for purposes
that are not consistent with its designated use.
The land provided by the local depot operator for the operation of our container depot in Dong Nai
province consists of parcels of land that are explicitly designated for aquaculture, perennial crops, other
seasonal crops, and urban residential land. Therefore, the land in question requires a conversion of land
use purpose before it can be leased. However, the local depot operator has not initiated the process to
obtain the necessary approval for such conversion as at the Latest Practicable Date.
Rectification actions and potential impact on us
As at the Latest Practicable Date, we were not aware of any actual or contemplated actions, claims
or investigations by any state authorities with respect to this land. Currently, to our Directors’ knowledge
and belief, most container depots in the greater Ho Chi Minh City area are operating on land that does not
have the appropriate land use right certificate. Nevertheless, we are actively exploring other suitable land
in the greater Ho Chi Minh City area to substitute the said land and to carry out our container depot
operations. It is estimated that relocation will lead to approximately one month of suspension of our
container depot operations, and the cost of relocation would be approximately US$300,000.
As advised by LNT & Partners, our legal advisers as to Vietnam law, the relevant state authorities
may (i) impose a fine of VND 20 million (equivalent to approximately S$1,000) on the local depot
operator; and (ii) require the local depot operator to return the misused land for which it has not obtained
the relevant land use right certificate, resulting in the cessation of our container depot operations at that
location. Any demand by the relevant state authorities for the recovery of the land must be made in
249

=== PAGE 259 ===
BUSINESS
accordance with statutorily prescribed procedures, whereby the relevant state authorities must first notify
the land owner of the contemplated recovery, together with instructions as to the handling of the
remaining property or land-attached assets (if any).
In light of above, our Directors consider that such non-compliance will not result in the cessation of
our container depot operations in Vietnam, and that the potential relocation will not have any material
adverse operational or financial impact on us.
Failure to make full contributions to the social insurance and housing provident fund
Background and reasons for non-compliance
During the Track Record Period and up to the Latest Practicable Date, (PRC) TJ Keyun did not
make full social insurance and housing provident fund contributions for its employees with an aggregate
shortfall of approximately RMB3.9 million (equivalent to approximately S$0.7 million), in accordance
with the Social Insurance Law and the Housing Provident Fund Regulations.
Our failure to make full contribution was mainly due to certain of our employees were not willing
to bear the costs associated with social insurance and housing provident fund contributions strictly in
proportion to their salaries received but rather receive compensation and benefits in lieu of such relevant
contributions.
Potential legal consequences and potential impact on us
It is estimated that for the years ended 31 December 2023, 2024 and 2025, the estimated aggregate
shortfall in social insurance contribution amounted to RMB1.2 million, RMB0.9 million and RMB0.6
million (equivalent to approximately S$0.2 million, S$0.2 million and S$0.1 million), respectively, and
the estimated aggregate shortfall in housing provident fund contribution amounted to RMB0.5 million,
RMB0.4 million and RMB0.3 million (equivalent to approximately S$0.1 million, S$0.1 million and
S$0.05 million), respectively. As of 31 December 2025, we have made no provision for such insufficient
contribution of social insurance and housing provident fund as our PRC Legal Advisers (Grandall) is of
the opinion that (i) the risk of (PRC) TJ Keyun being required to make up the shortfall of contribution of
social insurance and housing provident fund is remote; and (ii) the risk of (PRC) TJ Keyun being subject
to administrative penalties for underpayment during the Track Record Period is remote for the reasons
explained below.
As advised by our PRC Legal Advisers (Grandall), the legal consequences for the failure to fully
contribute the social insurance and housing provident fund under the relevant PRC laws and regulations
include: (i) with respect to the social insurance, we may be ordered by the competent authority to pay the
relevant outstanding social insurance contributions within a stipulated time period and may be required to
pay a late payment fee of up to 0.05% of the relevant outstanding amounts for each day of delay in
accordance with the Social Insurance Law; if we fail to pay the outstanding amounts and the late payment
fee as required, we may be imposed fines in an aggregate amount ranging from one to three times of the
relevant outstanding social insurance contribution; and (ii) with respect to the housing provident funds, in
accordance with the Housing Provident Fund Regulations, we may be ordered by the relevant authority to
pay the outstanding amounts within a prescribed time period, and if we fail to make such outstanding
amounts as required, we may be subject to an enforcement by relevant competent court.
